lines: Picture a churn model that looks genuinely strong the day it's evaluated offline.
Put the same model in front of real traffic, and it barely edges out a coin flip.
Nobody touched the model in between. So the model isn't where the problem lives.
Here's the actual question hiding underneath that gap.
When you build a training row, do you read a feature's value as it stands today, or as it stood at the exact moment the label happened?
Those can be two completely different numbers. Which one is the training set allowed to trust?
answer: It's tempting to say it shouldn't matter, since it's the same underlying data either way.
But a feature's value today already includes everything that happened since the label, including things the outcome itself caused.
Reading the value as of the label's own moment is the only version a live model will ever actually get to see.

lines: So here's the mechanism that enforces that discipline.
Start at the label's own timestamp, and scan backward in time.
Stop the instant you hit the first feature value sitting at or before that moment, and use that one, never a later one.
steps.takeaway: An as-of join doesn't ask what a feature is now. It asks what it was, the moment the label happened.

lines: Now watch that discipline matter, on a real dataset built for exactly this.
Join the labels to each feature's current value, train on it, and the resulting score looks excellent.
Join the same labels the correct way instead, scanning backward from each label's own moment, and that score drops hard.
Nothing about the model changed between those two runs. Only which value each join was allowed to see did.
steps.takeaway: The naive score was never a lie about the training data. It was the truth about data a live model will never have.

lines: Not every leak is a timing problem, though, and this next one proves it.
Picture a column that records why a customer cancelled, and notice it's only ever filled in for customers who already cancelled.
Scan backward from the label's own moment all you like. That column still has nothing in it yet, for anyone, because the thing it records hasn't happened.
steps.takeaway: Temporal leakage is a question of when you looked. This one is a question of why the field exists at all.

lines: One more pair of edge cases worth committing to before we measure them.
First, a label from before any feature value for that customer even exists yet.
Second, a label whose nearest feature value sits further back than the staleness limit you've set allows.
In both cases, what should the join actually hand back?
answer: It's tempting to grab the nearest value anyway, on the theory that something is better than nothing.
But past that stated limit, the honest answer is that the feature's state is unknown, not a convenient guess standing in for it.
So both cases should come back empty, and quietly substituting the nearest value would hide exactly the gap the limit exists to surface.

lines: Both of those cases, run for real, do exactly that.
A label with nothing earlier to scan back to comes back empty.
A label whose nearest value sits outside the staleness window also comes back empty, even though a value does technically exist further back.
steps.takeaway: A staleness limit isn't a performance setting. It's an admission that a feature's value can get too old to mean anything.

lines: One last way this can quietly go wrong, and it has nothing to do with timing at all.
Add a brand new feature to a model that's already live, and someone has to compute its history for every label that came before launch.
Do that backfill with the exact same transformation that runs online, from one shared piece of logic feeding both paths.
Approximate that transformation a second time instead, even with the best intentions, and you've quietly built two different features sharing one name.
steps.takeaway: A backfilled feature isn't close enough to the online version. If it isn't identical, it's a second feature wearing the first one's name.

lines: Pull the whole topic together.
Read every feature as of the label's own moment, never as of today.
Drop any field that only exists because the outcome already happened, since no amount of join timing rescues that one.
And respect a stated limit on how old known is allowed to be, rather than quietly filling the gap with a guess.
One last scenario, pulling all of this together.
A new feature gets added nine months after launch, and the engineer doing the backfill never had access to the original online code.
They approximate it instead, from the warehouse tables, doing their honest best.
Given everything you've just watched measured here, should that backfilled history be trusted as the same feature?
answer: It's tempting to assume the warehouse holds the same underlying facts, so close enough should be fine.
But without the exact transformation, that approximation is a plausible stand-in that can quietly diverge from what the live service actually computes.
That gap stays invisible until it shows up as a mismatch between what was served and what was trained on, which is precisely what the next topic sets out to measure directly.
